item.content:encoded:
Sidebar (@SidebarIO)

Your documentation is still in your Mum's filing cabinet https://gerireid.com/blog/organising-documentation-for-humans-and-ai/?ref=sidebar https://t.co/NEPA7TILXU

🔗 Your documentation is still in your Mum's filing cabinet

Your documentation is still in your Mum’s filing cabinet
It’s kind of wild when you stop and think about it.
Most documentation is arranged into files, folders and hierarchies. A document goes inside a folder inside another folder and on the surface it’s well tidy. The trouble is that knowledge rarely behaves that way.
A component accessibility decision can affect design, engineering, content and customer support. So where do you put the documentation for it? The more complex the subject, the more awkward that choice becomes.
The modern [desktop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desktop_metaphor) was developed at Xerox PARC in the 1970s. Early graphical user interfaces borrowed heavily from physical office concepts like documents, folders and filing systems because they were familiar to office workers.
Fifty years later, we’re still using the same mental model. But how many people under 30 have even used a physical filing cabinet?
The filing cabinet we inherited
We rarely stop to consider how much of our digital world is built on this old office metaphor.
I once worked with a guy who saved all his files directly on his Mac desktop. He navigated spatially, placing documents into different zones on the screen and developing a muscle memory for where they were located. I’m not sure he even realised they were saved within a directory structure underneath the desktop folder.
I grew up with the idea of documents inside folders, and as a UX designer, I just expanded on it to create the information architectures of websites.
But imagine if we hadn’t been primed with this tree structure? Maybe more creative and spatial interfaces would have emerged instead.
People don’t browse documentation like librarians
There’s a theory called [Information Foraging](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/information-foraging/), which suggests that people follow clues rather than systematically exploring hierarchies.
Peter Pirolli and Stuart Card describe people as information foragers. This is such a rad term for people looking for stuff on the web. Like a badger foraging for small invertebrates, we humans look for signs that useful information might be nearby and constantly decide whether to continue the search.
This may help explain why documentation users often:
- search before browsing
- stop after exploring a few levels
- ask a colleague instead
- create duplicate documents
The information often exists, but people don’t instinctively find where it has been stored. It made sense to the person setting up the filing cabinet, but because it’s several drawers down, nestled in with the winter jumpers and hiking socks, it was never to be found. We are all familiar with that team’s Confluence wiki.
Knowledge doesn’t fit into one folder
Circling back to design systems, a component accessibility decision might go in any drawer of the cabinet:
- design
- engineering
- content
- accessibility
- customer support
But our folder structure forces us to pick one location. The moment we do that, every other route becomes harder.
Researchers have been discussing this limitation for decades. Work on Semantic File Systems in the early 1990s argued that information should be retrievable through attributes and meaning rather than physical location. People usually think about information in terms of topics and tasks, while traditional file systems organise information by location.
AI exposes the problem
Compare this to how AI navigates. Most modern AI retrieval systems don’t rely primarily on folder structures in the way traditional document repositories do.
A design token page can be retrieved because it mentions colour contrast, not because it lives inside:
Design System → Foundations → Accessibility → Colour
The more I work with AI systems, the more obvious it becomes that folders are a storage mechanism, not a knowledge architecture. AI is exposing a problem that humans have been working around for years.
From storage architecture to knowledge architecture
We live in a wor

item.content:encoded:
eric zakariasson (@ericzakariasson)

##
To view keyboard shortcuts, press question mark
[View keyboard shortcuts](http://x.com/i/keyboard%5Fshortcuts)
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLugm-bX0AENCWc?format=jpg&name=900x900)](http://x.com/ericzakariasson/article/2070493377267646797/media/2070425045160153089)
Human in the /loop
[![](https://pbs.twimg.com/profile_images/1841151626456801283/HnXqy3TQ_normal.jpg)](http://x.com/ericzakariasson)
[eric zakariasson![](https://pbs.twimg.com/profile_images/1970182748146180096/dhZeXi_X_bigger.jpg)](http://x.com/ericzakariasson)
[@ericzakariasson](http://x.com/ericzakariasson)
·
3h
Follow
Click to Follow ericzakariasson
13
23
416
[24K](http://x.com/ericzakariasson/status/2070493377267646797/analytics)
What I like most about coding with agents right now is the room to leave a few runs going and still get on with other work. When something finishes or needs a call, I show up.
This post is a short explainer of the setup I use, a definition of done the agent can score, a loop that keeps going until it should stop, pings so I know when to lean in.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLuaKQ7WkAA6wQc?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/ericzakariasson/article/2070493377267646797/media/2070417954840154112)
##
Find something the agent can verify
Before kicking off a longer running task, I lock a definition of done. Examples I actually use:
* Model or eval work. Target is a score. Change the approach, run the eval, keep the change only if the number moved the right way. Closest to
[Karpathy's autoresearch](https://github.com/karpathy/autoresearch)
for ML training loops.
* Web app or UI. Target is a QA pass. Load the page or run Playwright, screenshot it, make sure it still does the thing.
* Backend or refactor. Target is the test suite. Failing tests first, then green, and it has to stay green.
* Speed or flakiness. Target is a number (p95, a benchmark). Change and measure until you're under the line you set.
* Data or content cleanup. Target is a count. Loop until zero rows fail validation, or every item passes the check.
Writing the loop is mostly writing how you'd check the work yourself. Some tasks need every step on the page. Others I give a goal and a rough direction and let the model fill in the middle. I start more explicit than I think I need, then loosen it once I see what it can infer.
##
Wrap it in a loop
Definition of done in hand, I tell the agent to loop on it. Change something, measure, keep or revert, go again. Doesn't have to be one tiny edit each time. The step just has to be measurable against the target. I care most about the stop conditions, which might be
* Metric hits the target
* No improvement after a few tries
* Out of ideas
* Blocked or unsure (stop and ask)
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLuaSKLXsAAhM79?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/ericzakariasson/article/2070493377267646797/media/2070418090467241984)
##
Get pinged instead of babysitting
So the agent gets a notify path (MCP plus /notify) and reaches me there. Usually Slack, because that's where everything else already is. Same setup could be iMessage or whatever. I treat it as a generic notification channel, not full Slack access for the agent. Status updates and "I need a decision" show up like normal messages. When I answer, that reply is the next thing the loop runs on.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLuaifqX0AAClYQ?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/ericzakariasson/article/2070493377267646797/media/2070418371112325120)
##
Run it in the cloud
Most of this doesn't stay on my laptop. It runs in the cloud so a loop can keep going for hours without my machine being open. I use my own client as the orchestrator and fan work out to cloud agents from there.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLubcL5W8AARmOW?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/ericzakariasson/article/2070493377267646797/media/2070419362238885888)
##
Then start the next one
Once a loop is running, I start anoth

Gorden Sun (@Gorden_Sun)

X上的这篇文章是我用Opus 4.6辅助写的。我还用豆包Seed 2.1 Pro写了一篇，发在了公众号上，可以对比看看：https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/TsyhPg2yyd5ccVahQVpt9A

🔗 Notion调研了6000个用AI的职场人：老板在自嗨，员工在装忙

Notion调研了6000个用AI的职场人：老板在自嗨，员工在装忙 原创 Gorden Sun Gorden Sun AI加速派 在小说阅读器读本章 去阅读 在小说阅读器中沉浸阅读 最近刷朋友圈是不是快焦虑死了？ 一会儿是"某公司用AI裁掉90%文案"，一会儿是"AI Agent已经能自己跑业务了"，再刷两篇"35岁不会AI就要被淘汰"的爆文，感觉明天就要被开除了。 但我跟你说， 这些都是假的。 Notion刚出了一份全球AI转型报告，调研了10个国家、6118个人——从拍板买AI的老板高管，到天天用AI干活的普通员工，给你扒了个底朝天。 看完你会发现：现在全网吹的AI革命，基本就是大型自嗨现场。 🤡 第一个真相：88%的公司，都在"假装用AI" 先给你看个最反常识的数据： 全球88%的公司，AI还停留在"个人玩具"阶段（Level 1+Level 2）。 什么意思？就是员工自己偷偷用ChatGPT写个文案、用AI做个PPT、开会让AI记个纪要、写代码让AI补个函数——说白了，就是拿AI当高级搜索+打字员用。 真正把AI嵌进公司业务流程、让AI自动跑重复工作的，只有10%（Level 3）。 至于网上吹得神乎其神的"AI自己开公司、自己做决策、全自动跑业务"—— 全地球只有2%的公司做到了。 对，你没看错，2%（Level 4）。 你刷到的那些天花乱坠的案例，全是这2%里的尖子生，剩下98%的公司，包括你我所在的大多数公司，都还在"用AI帮我写个周报"的阶段。 所以别焦虑了，真的。你觉得自己AI用得烂？没关系，你们老板、你们CEO，大概率也跟你差不多。 现在的AI转型，就像当年刚有电脑的时候——大家都买了电脑，但大部分人也就用来打打字、上上网，真正用电脑改造业务的，没几个。 第二个真相：老板和员工，根本活在两个世界 这是整个报告里最好笑、也最扎心的部分。 你知道老板眼里的公司AI用得怎么样吗？ ◆ 49%的老板说："我们公司AI用得贼溜，我非常有信心！" ◆ 60%的老板说："我们已经准备好上AI Agent了！" 那员工眼里呢？ ◆ 只有23%的员工觉得公司AI用得明白—— 差了一倍还多 ◆ 只有36%的员工觉得公司准备好了上AI Agent 更离谱的是什么？ 老板觉得自己公司26%的部门已经深度用AI了，员工说：拉倒吧， 只有5% 。 整整5倍的认知差！ 我给你翻译一下这是什么场景： 老板在大会上激情演讲："我们公司已经全面AI化了！效率提升300%！明年就要用AI再造一个公司！" 底下员工一边点头鼓掌，一边偷偷想："上周让我用的那个AI工具，写出来的东西全是错的，我改了俩小时，还不如自己写得快。" 为什么会这样？ 因为老板看到的是：我们买了多少AI工具，请了多少AI专家，开了多少AI培训——这都是钱花出去了。 员工感受到的是：这玩意儿不好用啊！写的东西有错，接不上公司的数据，出了问题谁负责也没人说，我用了还要担责任，那我不如不用。 最搞笑的是一个英国员工的吐槽："AI有时候就瞎编东西，编完了还跟我说'好眼力'，我本来想省时间，结果省下来的时间全用来给AI挑错了。" 是不是世另我？ 第三个真相：越投钱，越焦虑 你以为公司AI用得越好，就越从容？ 错了。 报告里说， 55%的老板都承认：我们投AI的速度，比员工学得快多了。 而且这个数字，随着AI用得越深，反而越高： ◆ 刚起步的公司：48%的老板觉得员工跟不上 ◆ 中级阶段：55% ◆ 深度应用：60% ◆ 最顶级的那批公司： 68% 说白了就是，老板们都在拼命砸钱上AI，生怕被时代落下，但员工根本接不住。 就像你给一个还在用功能机的人，直接塞了个最新款iPhone，还给他装了100个APP，说"你赶紧用，用不好你就被淘汰了"——他能不懵吗？ 而且最讽刺的是什么？ 现在几乎所有公司都在做AI培训、都在买标准化工具、都在写AI使用规范—— 但这些东西，根本拉不开差距。 因为所有公司都在做啊！你做我也做，最后大家又回到同一起跑线。 第四个真相：真正拉开差距的，根本不是你想的那样 那真正把那12%的先进公司和剩下88%拉开的，到底是什么？ 报告里测了8项指标，最后发现只有3件事有用，而且差距大到离谱： 1. 把AI嵌进你已经在用的系统里（+18%） 不是让员工再学10个新AI工具，而是把AI直接接进你天天用的飞书、钉钉、CRM、文档里。不用切换APP，打开就能用，这才是真的有用。此处我提名飞书CLI， 接入飞书CLI，才算真正用上了AI 。 2. 建清楚规矩和监管（+16%） 不是简单写个"不准泄密"就完了，而是要说清楚：AI出了错谁负责？哪些数据能给AI看？哪些工作AI做完必须人审？员工敢用了，才会真的用。 3. 别光吹"省了多少时间"，拿真金白银的数据说话（+15%） 别再听员工说"我用AI省了俩小时"这种鬼话了，真正的先进公司都在算：错误率降了多少？项目周期短了多少？到底省了多少钱、多赚了多少钱？ 看到没？ 不是培训没用，不是工具没用，而是这些都是基础分，大家都有。 真正能让你跑到前面的，是把AI从"员工个人的玩具"，变成"公司系统的一部分"。 🤦‍♂️ 第五个真相：AI用得越深，问题反而越奇葩 还有个特别有意思的发现： AI用得不好的时候，问题都是人的问题："我不会用"、"我不敢信"、"没人教我"。 等你AI真用深了，问题全变成系统的问题了： ◆ 工具太多了（+14%） ：公司买了一堆AI工具，写文案用这个，做表用那个，写代码用第三个，员工都不知道该用哪个 ◆ 不知道到底有没有用（+9%） ：钱花了不少，时间也投了，到底效率提升了多少？没人说得清 ◆ AI今天说的和明天不一样（+5%） ：模型版本一更新，输出结果就变了，根本没法稳定用 反而早期的那些问题：不会用、不敢信，随着用得多了，慢慢就解决了。 所以你看，根本不存在什么"等我准备好了再上AI"——你永远准备不好。 上了AI之后，只会有新的问题等着你。但解决了这些新问题，你就跑到前面去了。 最后：不管是公司还是个人，别瞎忙活了 看完这份报告，我最大的感受就是：现在的AI焦虑，90%都是炒出来的。 给公司老板们提个醒： 别再搞什么全员AI培训运动了，也别再买一堆工具回来就觉得自己转型了。 你先搞清楚三件事： 1. 别自己在办公室拍脑袋想AI怎么用，去问问一线员工，他们到底觉得哪里难用 2. 先别急着上新工具，把AI接到大家已经在用的系统里，比什么都强 3. 别再听"省了多少时间"这种屁话，拿错误率、周期、营收这些硬指标说话 给普通职场人提个醒： 真的别焦虑了。 现在88%的人都跟你一样，拿AI写写文案做做PPT，谁也别笑话谁。 你不用怕"不会AI就要被淘汰"，你只要比你同部门的人多走一步—— 比如别人只会让AI写文案，你会让AI帮你分析数据； 别人只会拿AI当聊天机器人，你会把自己的工作流和AI结合起来； 你就已经赢过90%的人了。 哦对了，还有个特别有意思的数据： 500-999人的中型公司，AI用得最好，反而5000人以上的大公司，AI转型最慢——因为船大难掉头。 所以别觉得大公司就一定走在前面，说不定你的小公司，反而能先跑出来。 最后问一句：你们公司AI用得怎么样？ 是不是老板天天喊AI转型，结果大家该怎么干活还怎么干活？ 评论区聊聊你们公司的AI魔幻现状，我看看是不是全世界都一个样。 *本文数据来源：Notion《2026全球AI转型报告》，调研样本覆盖10个国家6118名AI决策者与使用者。原报告链接：*https://www.notion.com/resources/inside-the-ai-transformation 预览时标签不可点 微信扫一扫 We’re leading a $4.3M seed round in Orthogonal to build the discovery and payments layer for the agentic economy.
##
The Problem
2026 is the first year AI agents such as Openclaw and Claude Code are entering the economy as real participants – writing code, sending emails, and closing tasks end to end. But the moment needs a capability or integration it wasn’t handed to complete a task, it hits a brick wall. An agent can't go find the right service, sign up, fetch a key, and start paying the way a person would. It fails, or worse, hallucinates results. Anyone who has spent a vibecoding session wrangling dashboards, juggling API keys, and reconciling spend across a dozen providers has felt this friction firsthand.
Today, discovery, access, and payments remain a blocker to agentic workflows. To truly unlock autonomous economic output, AI agents today still need to figure out how to use money and the Internet.
##
Enter Orthogonal
Orthogonal is building the bridge between agents and the rest of the Internet - creating a unified discovery layer for APIs that allow AI agents to better participate in the global economy. An agent such as OpenClaw and Claude puts in a single integration – whether through SDK, API, MCP, or CLI – and can start to search and discover capabilities it doesn’t have in-built.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLrf78YbQAAeWvm?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/0xfishylosopher/article/2070222427670618460/media/2070213199644016640)
Over the past few months, Orthogonal has built up a catalog of hundreds of endpoints from 50+ vendors across a variety of use cases, allowing agents to search for customer contacts, buy compute, generate images, and get access to email and phone numbers. Today, we already see Orthogonal enriching leads for marketing teams, running data analysis for investors, sourcing candidates for recruiters. In a single call, builders integrate once and get everything – a single account with authorization and unified invoicing across every provider, and ability for agents to pay using stablecoins and protocols such as x402.
##
Meet the Team
Orthogonal has exactly the right team we look for at this layer. Cofounder and CEO
[Christian Pickett](https://www.linkedin.com/in/christian-pickett/)
has spent his career building payments and billing infrastructure – payments at Coinbase, usage-based billing at Vercel – and is sharply aware of where the market is today versus where it's heading. Co-founder
[Bera Sogut](https://www.linkedin.com/in/berasogut/)
built APIs and autonomous systems at scale, having worked on reCAPTCHA and Maps APIs at Google, and ranks among the strongest competitive programmers in the world. Both cofounders know payments and APIs inside-out, and are in the best position to build the payments and API discovery gateway for the agentic economy.
##
Our Thesis
As AI agents enter the workforce as full participants, a new agentic economy is taking shape, and we believe Orthogonal will become a cornerstone of the agentic stack.
The tasks of the future will require agents to conduct long-horizon, multi-API, and multi-protocol search, payme

item.content:encoded:
George Grigorev (@iamgrigorev)

The moment you know it’s gonna be great read from legendary writer

https://lilianweng.github.io/posts/2026-06-24-scaling-laws/

🔗 Scaling Laws, Carefully | Lil'Log

Scaling laws are one of the most critical empirical findings in deep learning. The observation is simple in form: the training loss $L$ decreases predictably as we scale up model size $N$, dataset size $D$, and compute $C$, following a power-law curve, which appears as a straight line on a log-log plot. We can view scaling laws as a framework for describing the relationship between compute, loss, model size and data; at its core, it is about how to allocate precious compute optimally between $N$ and $D$.
This predictability makes scaling laws highly valuable in practice. A common workflow is to fit scaling laws on a handful of small runs and then extrapolate to estimate the token and compute requirements for larger models.
| Symbol | Note |
|---|---|
| $N$ | Model size, measured in parameter count. |
| $D$ | Training dataset size, usually measured in token count. |
| $C$ | Training compute in FLOPs. As a useful approximation, $C \approx 6ND$ ( [Kaplan et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361)), where $2ND$ accounts for the forward pass and $4ND$ for backpropagation. |
| $E$ | Irreducible loss |
| $L, \hat{L}(.)$ | Test loss / test loss prediction function; can also refer to training loss, since they are strongly correlated. |
| $\epsilon$ | Generalization error. |
Early days: ML loss predictability[#](https://lilianweng.github.io#early-days-ml-loss-predictability)
The predictability of generalization error with scale had already been investigated before scaling laws became a mainstream concept.
[Amari et al. (1992)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/6796972) derived four types of learning curves using a Bayesian approach and the annealed approximation.
- Deterministic learning algorithm, noiseless data, one unique solution: $\epsilon \sim c \cdot D^{-1}$, where $c$ is some constant.
- Deterministic learning algorithm, noiseless data, multiple equivalent solutions: $\epsilon \sim c \cdot D^{-2}$; the learning is faster with each new data point, because the model only learns the optimal manifold of parameters, instead of finding the single solution point.
- Deterministic learning algorithm, noisy data: $\epsilon \sim c \cdot D^{-1/2}$; noises in data make learning harder.
- Stochastic learning algorithm, noisy data: $\epsilon \sim c \cdot D^{-1} + E$; here the irreducible loss $E$ is the residual error that a stochastic learner cannot reduce further, for example when the model runs out of capacity on large data. All four types of learning curves follow a power law:
where $E$ can be 0 and $\alpha = -2, -1, -1/2$. Although their theoretical setup is based on a simplified binary classification task, it points in a useful direction for building empirical ML loss prediction models.
One of the earliest empirical studies by [Hestness et al. (2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.00409) explained the relationship between generalization error, model size and data. For a given training data size, they identified the best-fit model size via grid search and then plotted loss against training dataset size. Across four different domains in deep learning (neural machine translation, image classification, language modeling, and speech recognition), a recurring pattern was observed where:
- Generalization error scales as a power law across a set of factors (e.g. data size).
- Model improvements shift the error curve but do not seem to affect the power-law exponent.
- Interestingly, architecture changes the offset ($E$) of the power-law fit but does not change the exponent ($\alpha$). The slope of the power law appears to be a property of the problem domain rather than the model architecture.
- The number of model parameters $N$ needed to fit a dataset of size $D$ also scales as a power law.
A conceptual illustration breaks the learning curve into three stages. In the small-data region, when there are not enough learning signals, the model performs only slightly better than random guessing. In the middle (“power-law region”), we observ

item.content:encoded:
Ian Johnson (@iandenisjohnson)

Thanks to the @ForeignAffairs editing staff for their great work on this piece, a review of Xu Guoqi’s extremely insightful book on Chinese identity.
(Gift link)
https://www.foreignaffairs.com/guest-pass/redeem/zDWmVXl_BT8

🔗 Who Is China? Who Is China? | Foreign Affairs

To many in the West, China’s rise is an indisputable fact. Commentators celebrate its success in language not seen since an earlier generation of political tourists gushed over Mao’s China: in February, after returning from a visit to the country, the investor and columnist Steven Rattner averred that China’s “model of state-directed capitalism” had helped produce “the colossus that dominates global manufacturing while making extraordinary progress in fast-growing, technology-oriented fields that have long been American led.” The economic historian Adam Tooze declared last year that the country “is the master key to understanding modernity.” Others seem resigned to asking narrow, technocratic questions: Will its military be ready to invade Taiwan next year, or a few years down the road? Can its authoritarian political model provide a stable succession when Chinese leader Xi Jinping dies? Can it overcome sanctions and produce cutting-edge chips? In doing so, they treat the permanency of the People’s Republic of China as a foregone conclusion.
What’s often lost in these discussions is that the country’s own leaders implicitly doubt the very concept of their nation. Government officials and many ordinary people vehemently proclaim the sanctity of China’s borders, even as many of its border regions are run under a state of near-martial law. Official narratives, meanwhile, forbid a coherent explanation of how [China](https://www.foreignaffairs.com/regions/china) obtained these lands. As part of a broader intellectual decay, many of the country’s brightest minds have exiled themselves, either through inner emigration and self-censorship or by leaving the country altogether.
China shouldn’t have much of an identity crisis. It boasts an ancient civilization and culture instantly recognizable around the world. Its intellectual inheritance—rich traditions in martial arts, medicine, philosophy, and religion—is widely admired and imitated in global popular culture and the high arts. But Chinese leaders behave as if they were running an upstart nation with no history—one that has to demand that visitors refer to it as “the People’s Republic” and repeat that there is only “one China,” located within sacred and immutable borders. The country today “is a multiheaded creature of no certain or reliable identity,” Xu Guoqi writes in his new book, The Idea of China: A Contested History. “If there were a clear or reliable identity, today’s leaders would not be so obsessed with trying to impose one.”
In the nearly 15 years since Xi took power, in 2012, he has tried to define China by fusing the glories of communism—sacrifice, duty, perseverance—and some elements of traditional culture, especially filial piety and obedience. But by emptying both of these ideologies of their subversive kernels—their emphasis on social justice and the right to disobedience, to name two—Xi has failed to construct a convincing vision of what China stands for. It remains unclear whether Xi’s version of China has any values beyond holding on to the territories of the old Qing empire and keeping the Chinese Communist Party in power, or whether the CCP’s project is capacious enough to accommodate the country’s historical hybridity.
To Xu, the party’s answer—building a “house of cards” atop the country’s multifarious history—could be its downfall. In the Soviet Union, a similar attempt to build a modern nation-state on the foundations of an empire fell apart after its leaders could not resolve the inherent contradictions of such a project. The CCP, The Idea of China suggests, might meet a similar fate if it does not change course.
The political and economic success of the last four decades will likely prevent the People’s Republic from collapsing like the Soviet Union. Still, Xu’s book should make one skeptical about the assumption that the China that exists today is the China that will exist long into the future. Instead, Xu reminds readers of the different possible paths C

This second post in the video modeling series focuses on architectures and training. Architectures for state-of-the-art video models are all based on the same basic recipe: a diffusion transformer backbone, which is adapted for various forms of conditioning (text, images, depth, pose, actions, etc.).
##
Basic architecture: video diffusion transformer
The basic video model architecture has remained very stable since the emergence of diffusion transformers (DiTs; Peebles & Xie ‘22). As described in the first post in this series, the raw video is transformed into a compact latent representation through the video VAE. The DiT patchifies this latent tensor using a 3D convolution. The patch representations are then passed through transformer blocks and then unpatchified. This pipeline is visualized below.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLqVtgHWAAAu4sm?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/Majumdar%5FAni/article/2070155053965480432/media/2070131587677552640)
Diffusion/flow timestep embedding. Video models are trained with the flow matching objective (Albergo ‘22, Lipman ‘22, Liu ‘22). Hence, the DiT above predicts the velocity at a given flow timestep. Timestep conditioning is performed via adaptive layer norm (adaLN), as proposed in the original DiT paper. Specifically, the timestep is encoded via an MLP, which produces the scale and shift parameters for layer norm (Ba ‘16). However, this method of conditioning introduces a very large number of parameters (since the MLP’s output must match the model width). An interesting twist in the WAN model (WAN team ‘25) is to get around this by sharing an MLP across the different transformer blocks (while keeping the bias term independent for different blocks). This reduces their overall parameter count by 25%.
Text encoder and conditioning. The text prompt is typically encoded through a version of the T5 encoder (Raffel ‘19) or a VLM. In recent video models, the DiT blocks of the video model condition on the text embedding through cross attention. In the past, other possibilities for text conditioning were explored (e.g., processing text and images through parallel streams and sharing information via attention; MM-DiT, Esser ‘24). However, LTX-Video (HaCohen ‘24) found that cross attention improved text conditioning compared to MM-DiT, and this is now the standard choice.
##
Architectures for controllable video generation
![](https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2070131829588312064/img/srjgdus73i0_Luz4.jpg)
Video transfer example from WAN-Animate.
Beyond text conditioning, modern video models allow for various forms of controllable generation: reference images or videos, pose, depth, etc. This allows for capabilities such as the one shown above from the WAN-Animate model (Cheng ‘25), where a character in the reference video is swapped with one shown in a reference image.
Below, I discuss various ways in which such control signals are introduced into video models.
ControlNet
ControlNet (Zhang ‘23) is a hugely influential method for controllable image and video generation. ControlNet freezes the parameters of the pre-trained base model and clones them into a trainable copy. This copy accepts the additional conditioning (e.g., pose, depth, edges) as input, and is connected to the frozen backbone u

item.content:encoded:
Bilgin Ibryam (@bibryam)

How I use LLMs as a staff engineer in 2026
https://www.seangoedecke.com/how-i-use-llms-in-2026

The biggest AI workflow change in 2026: treating agents as capable collaborators for coding, debugging, testing, and codebase research—while still keeping humans responsible for judgment, communication, and review.

🔗 How I use LLMs as a staff engineer in 2026

How I use LLMs as a staff engineer in 2026
A bit over a year ago I wrote [How I use LLMs as a staff engineer](https://www.seangoedecke.com/how-i-use-llms/). Here’s a brief summary of what I used AI for last year:
- Smart autocomplete with Copilot
- Short tactical changes in areas I don’t know well (always reviewed by a SME)
- Writing lots of use-once-and-throwaway research code
- Asking lots of questions to learn about new topics (e.g. the Unity game engine)
- Last-resort bugfixes, just in case it can figure it out immediately
- Big-picture proofreading for long-form English communication
Here are some tasks I explicitly didn’t use AI for last year:
- Writing whole PRs for me in areas I’m familiar with
- Writing ADRs or other technical communications
- Research in large codebases and finding out how things are done
February 2025 was a long time ago. Back then the best model was the first reasoning model, OpenAI’s o1. Agents sort of worked, but would often get stuck or thrown off by compaction. What’s changed since then?
Agents are good now
The biggest change is that I now use LLMs to produce entire PRs in areas I’m familiar with. A year ago I would very occasionally ask an agent to make changes to a single file if it was a simple change I couldn’t be bothered typing out. Sometimes I would copy a function I wrote into a LLM chat window for feedback. But now I start every single change by asking an agent to solve the problem, and usually push the PR after a single editing pass.
In late 2025 I used a lot of open VSCode windows. In early 2026, that changed to terminal tabs with the Copilot CLI, particularly when I needed to make changes across multiple repos at the same time. Now I use the [GitHub Copilot app](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-05-14-github-copilot-app-is-now-available-in-technical-preview/) a lot (tens of sessions per day).
This reflects a shift from having to line-edit the agent basically as it went to only doing an editing pass right at the end. Early agents would go wrong a lot and not be able to recover, so it was valuable to keep an eye on their thought processes and step in to pause them and set them right. In my experience, current agents move too fast to do this, and recover their own mistakes most of the time anyway.
Sometimes I don’t even need to make edits and I can just push the change as-is, though this is rare: if nothing else, I typically go through and remove some of the over-commenting and other LLM-isms.
I do a lot of skimming through and evaluating agent changes. Most of the time I reject them entirely, just based on “eh, that’s not what I was thinking”. On average it takes me about thirty seconds to make this initial assessment. If the change looks alright after that, I’ll dig in and do a proper review to make sure I understand it and it’s doing the right thing. For difficult tasks, I’ll often reject five or six (or more!) agent attempts before accepting one as good enough to work with, or giving up and making the change by hand.
Investigating bugs
I rely on LLMs even more for bug-hunting than I do for making changes. In 2025, I used to throw the occasional bug at a LLM, just in case it was able to rapidly come up with an explanation. Now I throw every bug at a LLM (typically by opening a new agent session and pasting in the bug report), because it’s able to correctly diagnose 80% of issues on its own. Current agents are really good at chasing down bugs, particularly when you give them a vantage point across multiple repositories.
I’m still better at it. Just last week I had a tricky bug that took about fourteen agent sessions before one finally figured it out. What was I doing in between and around those sessions?
- Digging up extra context on the bug (from logs, Slack, etc) and reporting it to the agents
- Building my own mental model of the problem, of course
- Setting up my own reproduction of the bug (in parallel with the agents’ efforts)
- Responding to agent sessions with “no, your the

When you watch someone ship three times your output with the same Claude Code, it's tempting to assume they know a magic prompt. They don't.
What they have is structure. Under the hood, the people getting the most out of Claude Code aren't typing better, they're running loops, small self-checking cycles that do the repetitive work for them. And it's not one clever loop. It's four distinct ones, each operating at a different timescale, from "every edit" to "across sessions."
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLuwIOvX0AAoZAm?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/0xMortyx/article/2070450974708093229/media/2070442109149106176)
Most people run zero of them. Seniors run all four, often without thinking of them as separate things. Here are the 4 loops, what each one does, and the exact way to add it to your own setup.
##
1\. The Edit/Test Loop
Runs on every change. Catches breakage the instant it happens.
Stop hook
The fastest loop, and the one most people skip. A senior doesn't trust an edit until the tests pass, and they don't run the tests by hand, a hook does it. A Stop hook runs your check as a script and blocks the turn from ending until it passes. The agent literally can't call a change "done" while the suite is red.
Because it's a hook, it's deterministic. It fires every single time, not the times Claude remembers to. That's the difference between "usually tested" and "always tested."
python
```python
.claude/settings.json // THE EDIT/TEST LOOP
{
"hooks": {
"Stop": [{
"command": "npm run test && npm run lint"
}]
}
}
# the turn can't end until tests and lint pass
# red suite = the agent keeps working, automatically
```
> ✓ Every change is verified the moment it's made, with zero effort from you
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLuwiKwXoAAvmq0?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/0xMortyx/article/2070450974708093229/media/2070442554756145152)
##
2\. The Goal Loop
Runs across many turns until a condition you wrote is true.
/goal
The edit/test loop guards a single change. The goal loop drives a whole task to completion on its own. You set a target and Claude Code keeps working, turn after turn, until that target is met: reading the failure, fixing it, re-checking, repeating, without you driving each lap.
The key detail that makes it trustworthy: the model that wrote the code doesn't get to decide whether it's done. A separate, faster model checks the completion condition after each turn. The doer does, a different judge confirms.
python
```python
THE GOAL LOOP
/goal All tests in test/ pass with no skips, and lint is clean
/loop until: the goal condition holds
# Claude reads failing output, traces it, edits, re-runs,
# and repeats on its own until the condition checks out
# a separate model grades "done", so it can't fake it
```
> The rule seniors follow here:A goal is only as good as the evidence that proves it. "Make the checkout better" gives the loop nothing to grade, so it stops whenever it feels like it. State the end state, the evidence required, and a hard ceiling on turns or budget. You write the acceptance test, the agent has to pass it.
> ✓ A whole task runs to a verified finish line while you do something else

🔗 Trump Administration Allows Anthropic to Release Mythos to Select US Organizations | WIRED

The US government has eased the restrictions it imposed on Anthropic’s most advanced AI model, [Claude Mythos 5](https://www.wired.com/story/anthropic-releases-claude-fable-5-mythos-5/), allowing the company to grant access to more than 100 US organizations, including large corporations and government agencies.
In a letter sent to Anthropic’s cofounder and chief compute officer Tom Brown obtained by WIRED, US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told the AI lab it would permit certain trusted partners to access Mythos because he had “determined that appropriate safeguards are in place.” Semafor first [reported](https://www.semafor.com/article/06/27/2026/us-releases-powerful-anthropic-model-mythos-to-some-us-companies) the existence of the letter.
“Anthropic has worked with the U.S. government to address risks associated with the Covered Models. These efforts have yielded significant progress,” Lutnick wrote.
However, the government stopped short of permitting a broader rollout of the model, and said nothing about the fate of Claude Fable 5, the consumer-facing version of Mythos that Anthropic released with significant additional safeguards. Lutnick noted in his letter that the other requirements outlined in the [initial directive](https://www.wired.com/story/anthropic-says-us-government-ordered-it-to-shut-down-mythos-models/) he sent on June 12 remain in effect.
“We received notice from the US government that Mythos 5, our strongest cybersecurity model, can be redeployed to a small group of cyber defenders and infrastructure providers,” Anthropic spokesperson Eduardo Maia Silva said in a statement to WIRED. “We are working to provision the approved set of providers and restore their access to Mythos 5 as quickly as possible. We are pleased to see this progress and continue to work with the government to expand access to Mythos 5 and make Fable 5 available for general use again.”
Anthropic is still in discussions with the White House about restoring access to Fable 5, and they are expected to continue over the weekend, according to a person familiar with the matter. Both parties are hopeful the resolution of this incident will help inform a lasting policy framework for future model releases, the person said.

| Are you a current or former Anthropic or US government employee who wants to talk about what's happening? We'd like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporter securely on Signal at mzeff.88 |
The partial reinstatement comes roughly two weeks after the White House sent an [export control directive to Anthropic](https://www.wired.com/story/anthropic-says-us-government-ordered-it-to-shut-down-mythos-models/) that required the company to limit foreign nationals from accessing Mythos and Fable 5, including people working and living in the United States. In response, Anthropic disabled access to the models entirely. In his latest letter, Lutnick wrote that organizations approved to use Mythos may now allow their foreign national employees to access the model, and Anthropic may do the same for its own foreign national employees.
The Trump administration grew concerned about Anthropic’s rollout of Mythos after it learned the company granted access to a [South Korean telecommunications firm](https://www.wired.com/story/sk-telecom-anthropic-mythos-export-controls/) it believed had ties to China, WIRED previously reported. Amazon and the National Security Agency also separately raised concerns to the White House that Fable 5 could be jailbroken, and the confluence of events convinced officials they needed to take action.
In recent weeks, Anthropic sent [senior members from its cybersecurity and AI safety teams to Washington, DC](https://www.wired.com/story/anthropic-is-still-at-odds-with-the-white-house-over-claude-fable-5/) to meet with Trump administration officials. Along with Brown, Anthropic's public policy chief Sarah Heck have been [leading the company’s discussions](https:/

item.content:encoded:
Bhumi Tharoor (@bhumikatharoor)

“Students have a deeper understanding of thorny concepts when they discuss and debate them together, and feel inspired to care more about mastering quadratic equations when they see their peers are trying to do the same” Jenny Anderson & Mike Goldstein https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/2026/06/ai-tutor-education-human-investment/687678/

🔗 AI Can’t Fix the Student-Motivation Problem - The Atlantic

In a 2023 [TED Talk](https://www.ted.com/talks/sal_khan_how_ai_could_save_not_destroy_education) watched by millions of people, the American educator and entrepreneur Sal Khan declared that AI was about to deliver “probably the biggest positive transformation that education has ever seen.” The founder and CEO of Khan Academy was touting the company’s new educational chatbot, Khanmigo, claiming it promised to be an “amazing personal tutor” to “every student on the planet.” By 2024, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was chiming in [that](https://ia.samaltman.com/) AI was on the verge of delivering, for students, “virtual tutors who can provide personalized instruction in any subject, in any language, and at whatever pace they need.”
But by this spring, Khan had [admitted that the release of Khanmigo](https://www.chalkbeat.org/2026/04/09/sal-khan-reflects-on-ai-in-schools-and-khanmigo/) was “a non-event” for many kids. Although access exploded, from reaching 40,000 students in 2023 to nearly 1 million this year, actual uptake—whether students use it—has stagnated.
A tool designed to respond to questions and ask follow-ups can’t help a student who doesn’t engage or know what to ask. Khanmigo, like so many other ed-tech tools, has floundered because it hasn’t solved the challenge at the center of education: How do you motivate students to experience the discomfort of learning something new? An AI tutor may be able to deliver math problems that are perfectly calibrated to a student’s level. But it can’t make the student actually do the problems.
“Learning is hard work,” Kristen DiCerbo, Khan Academy’s chief learning officer, told us. “It’s cognitively effortful and not experienced as fun. How do we get kids to want to do that?” AI is a powerful tool, she added, but it can’t be expected “to bridge that motivation gap.” Although AI tutors have sometimes [proven](https://blog.khanacademy.org/what-a-randomized-control-trial-in-uttar-pradesh-india-teaches-us-about-improving-math-learning-with-khan-academy/) [valuable](https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/099548105192529324/pdf/IDU-c09f40d8-9ff8-42dc-b315-591157499be7.pdf) in low-resource schools in developing countries, a recent [Stanford review](https://scale.stanford.edu/sites/default/files/The%20Evidence%20Base%20on%20AI%20in%20K-12%20Report.pdf) of all of the available research into the use of AI in K–12 schools found that educational benefits for students generally were limited.
Only about one in three students is highly engaged in school, [according](https://www2.census.gov/library/publications/2026/demo/p70-212.pdf) to U.S. census data—a share that has remained stable over the past decade. These students, who also tend to come from wealthier homes with two educated parents, may well be motivated to seek extra guidance from a bot. But a motivated minority will not produce a revolution.
Even among the driven few, only a fraction of kids use ed-tech tools such as Khanmigo enough to see any gains. Laurence Holt, the author of [The Science of Tutoring](https://scienceoftutoring.com/), [calls this the 5 percent problem](https://www.educationnext.org/5-percent-problem-online-mathematics-programs-may-benefit-most-kids-who-need-it-least/): About 5 percent of students use education technology as intended, thus reaping the learning benefits. That means that instead of democratizing access to affordable tutors, these tools could very well [widen inequality](https://ideas.repec.org/a/nas/journl/v123y2026pe2507708123.html) by supercharging students who are already motivated to get ahead.
Personalized 24-hour systems and adaptive algorithms held such promise, but apparently no amount of animation or gamification will convince a student to care about learning if they don’t already. Khan has lately hedged any talk of a digital transformation. “I think our biggest lever is really investing in the human systems,” he said in a Chalkbeat interview in April.
Essentially, these ed-tech experiments have drive

I have used Cursor, Claude, ChatGPT Codex, and OpenCode. The model changes every 3 months and the harness changes every 6 months, but my workflow has not changed once.
The workflow ships code in any language, through any tool, with any model. The tool does not matter. The model does not matter. The workflow is the constant.
Here are the 6 moves, brother.
#
The baseline - every agent follows these three
These are not negotiable. I do not start a session without them.
##
Move 1: Web search before the agent guesses.
The agent will hallucinate an API before it admits it does not know one, brother - like a friend giving you directions to a restaurant they have never been to, describing the building in detail, the street name, the cross street, and the color of the awning, all completely made up. I let it search the web first - real docs, real issue threads, real example code. The difference between a hallucinated fix and a real fix is one search query, and most agent configurations disable web search or restrict it to the repo when a 30-second search would have saved 30 minutes of wrong code.
##
Move 2: A reasoning break after every three failures.
The agent will try, fail, try something slightly different, fail again, and repeat 12 times without asking why. I force a stop after every third failure and demand analysis - what pattern do you see in your failures? Are you repeating the same approach? Do you understand why the test suite rejected you? Without this, the agent is a hamster wheel with better insulation.
##
Move 3: A brainstorming gate before any file is touched.
The agent sees a problem and starts editing within seconds because it does not know that it does not understand the problem. I force it to report what it found, explain the approach in plain terms, and wait for approval before touching a single file. This catches more wrong turns than any test suite, because the agent's plan reveals that it was about to edit the wrong file in the wrong crate.
#
The differentiators - these are what make it work across languages and tools
The baseline stops the agent from wasting time. These three make the agent actually productive.
##
Move 4: Research the ecosystem before writing a single line.
When I work in a language I know, the agent follows my conventions. When I work in a language I am exploring, I do something the prompt guides never mention - I let the agent research popular repositories in that language, identify their best practices, and adopt them as the convention for this session.
Then I create a skill graph - simple, connected skills that the agent follows for this specific language and project. Not an Obsidian vault. Not a web of notes. Just the skills the agent needs, connected by dependencies, small enough to fit in context, complete enough that the agent never needs to guess the conventions.
The first time I worked in Zig, the agent found the standard patterns from the compiler's own codebase and applied them before I knew what the patterns were. The first time I worked in C++ with this workflow, the agent learned the project's smart pointer policy from the existing code and never suggested a raw pointer.
##
Move 5: 100 lines or one feature per file. And grouping happens before creation.
A file should be 100 lines or one feature, whichever comes first, brother

item.content:encoded:
h100envy (@h100envy)

Here is a condensed, high-impact version of the post:

Discover -> Hand off -> Verify -> Persist -> Schedule

This 12-page PDF completely changed how I build agentic systems. Here is the 5-step blueprint:

Discovery: The loop reads CI, issues, and commits to find what's worth fixing.

Handoff: Each finding gets an isolated git worktree so parallel agents never collide.

Verification: A second agent - built to assume the code is broken, reviews the work.

Persistence: Results land on disk, never in a temporary context window.

Scheduling: Automation fires the entire process on a timer, making it a true loop.

The key insight: An agent grading its own work always praises it. You need that second agent to say "no."

Read it now, then explore the article below.

tl;dr - Agents that learn like people (through experience, teaching, & self-study) will be powered by memory models: models specialized in creating and curating token-space memory that transfers across model generations, trained with memory-native RL.
Memory is the key to unlocking AI agents that are not only teachable, but also capable of continually learning and self-improving. Techniques for continual learning in
[token space](https://www.letta.com/blog/continual-learning/)
have seen widespread real-world adoption, with agentic memory management, agent dreaming, and skill learning becoming central features in agent harnesses such as Letta Code, Claude Code, DeepAgents, and OpenClaw. Token-space learning takes advantage of the in-context learning capabilities of modern LLMs, which continue to improve across model generations, and provides an incredibly data-efficient mechanism for continual learning.
However, while LLMs are excellent at using context, they do not reliably create durable context for future tasks. This can lead to memory rot over time for long-lived agents, and limit the extent to which agents can learn independently from available context or past experience. We believe that advancing and scaling token-space learning will require a new type of specialized memory models, specifically designed for creating memory and expertise that transfers across models.
#
The memory & learning problem for agents
Through memory and learning, agents should be able to develop expertise over time based on their own unique experiences and the context made available to them. Without the capability to learn from experience, agents have clear limitations in use cases such as:
* Adapting to proprietary datasets and workflows: Even when agents have access to proprietary data and other private knowledge, they have a limited ability to condition their behavior on it. While forms of
[sleep-time compute](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13171)
like
[self-study](https://jacobxli.com/blog/2026/machine-studying/)
and
[skill learning](https://www.letta.com/blog/skill-learning/)
allow for turning private datasets into compact reusable contexts, existing methods are too expensive to scale to large corpuses and suffer from issues such as overgeneralization and memory rot.
* Embedding human expertise for digital cloning: Agent learning today is insufficient to fully absorb the expertise and values of human teachers or to create a true “digital clone” of humans. Approaches like skills and persona prompting can embed specialized behavior in agents, but agents today still remain far less capable than humans at learning and adapting from natural language feedback and real-world interactions.
* Deep personalization: Even with clearly stated preferences, feedback, or other personal information, agents struggle to recall relevant context and generate new memories. This constrains how personalized agent experiences can become for individual users, as agents are limited in their ability to learn from their interactions with users despite an abundance of interaction data.
Solving the memory and learning problem unlocks a new scaling axis for machine intelligence, since agents can continually improve by scaling compute on context. The more time an agent spends refining their memory and context,

Most outbound teams cannot tell you which part of their machine actually produced revenue.
That blind spot is what quietly kills good programs.
The budget gets cut in the wrong place, while nobody can prove what was working underneath.
We have sent more than 23 million cold emails across 2,200 campaigns for 400+ B2B companies at ColdIQ. The programs that compound all share one unglamorous trait: their pipeline traces back to the exact source and signal that produced it, automatically, without anyone exporting a spreadsheet.
This is the playbook for engineering that, from the data model up.
#
The metrics most teams watch are the ones that lie
Goodhart's Law is the whole problem in one sentence: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLliccXa4AAl54_?format=png&name=small)](http://x.com/itsalexvacca/article/2070189941209075906/media/2069793744543735808)
The moment a team starts optimizing for meetings booked or emails sent, those numbers detach from revenue and begin flattering everyone who reports them.
> The current spectator metric is "agents built" or "emails sent." Both are vanity.
The vanity number does little harm sitting in a dashboard. The harm starts when people act on it.
A calendar full of meetings nobody can close still renders as a healthy chart. A budget that is quietly carrying the whole motion gets cut because its line item looks expensive when you read it in isolation.
I watched exactly that play out the first time we ran ads and outbound as separate functions with separate scorecards.
> Separate dashboards let the finance team kill the ads budget the first time the cost-per-meeting line looks high, while missing that the outbound reply rate is lifting precisely because that budget is funding the warming layer.
Attribution engineering exists to remove that blindness.
The goal is a system where every dollar of pipeline is wired back to the source and the signal that created it, so the decisions about what to cut and what to fund get made on evidence instead of on whichever number happened to load first.
#
What attribution engineering actually means
Reporting describes what happened after the fact. Attribution engineering builds the plumbing that makes the description true and automatic.
The distinction matters because a report assembled by hand once a month is always stale and always a little wrong, whereas a system that stamps every touch as it happens is already correct by the time anyone opens it.
There is a hard requirement underneath all of it.
The data has to move from the ad platform through the CRM and into the sequencer on its own, every week, without anyone exporting spreadsheets by hand.
Everything in this playbook is built to satisfy that one requirement.
##
Step 1: Instrument the funnel as a series of events
Before you can attribute anything, you need a clean set of events that every account passes through, each one captured the moment it happens.
The stages we instrument are deliberately simple, running from the first message sent, to a reply coming back, to a meeting booked, to an opportunity created, to a deal closed.
Each of those becomes a timestamped event written to a single place, rather than a status that lives in whatever tool happened to record it.

For all of us who love to imagine, discover, and build, this is a new golden age with boundless opportunities ahead. Artificial intelligence is beginning to change what it means to do science, to be an engineer - to fulfill some of the oldest promises: To build a machine radically smarter than us, with agency in the world, to ultimately build a better world for all of us. It acts as a participant in the work itself: reading the literature, proposing ideas, writing and running the code to test them, experimenting in the physical world, and learning from what works and what does not. The most consequential applications of this will be in discovery, to expand on human-generated knowledge more rapidly than any other technology has been able to. One of the most promising but also challenging applications is in materials science: in the slow, expensive, intuition-bound process by which we find the new molecules, materials, and mechanisms that our future depends on.
This marks a shift in paradigm: The conventional approach was to train a model on the corpus of existing science - a powerful move, but one that yields, by construction, a compression of what is already known: asked a question, the model returns the consensus of its training distribution. The new frontier of discovery AI inverts this. Rather than only learning from data we already have, these systems generate their own - proposing candidates, running simulations and experiments, and turning the results into fresh data that did not exist before. The model stops being a mirror of the literature and becomes an engine that actively extends it. Genuine discovery is the production of claims that lie outside the current picture, often in direct tension with it. The history of science is a history of results that contradicted the prevailing world model and turned out to be true - because they explained observations better, enabled radically new engineering, and let us imagine new products. So discovery is to expand from what we have seen to dramatically new terrain.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLo9XevWIAEhCOM?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/ProfBuehlerMIT/article/2070218465491972248/media/2070034452328095745)
Scientific workflows from isolated tool used to decentralized systems. F. Wang, M. Buehler et al.
We need systems that can extend the boundary of the known: To propose something the state of the art does not contain, recognize when a result conflicts with their own priors, and then do the thing a search engine never does: prove it. Discovery requires a model that is willing to be wrong about itself, that can recognize this breaking point, and which treats its own world model as a hypothesis to be falsified. A system that proposes freely, then testing each proposal against physical law, simulation, and experiment, and updating when the test comes back against expectation. A discovery is only a discovery once it has survived an attempt to break it, and when it demonstrably and irreversibly changes the world.
![](https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2070034783489445888/img/AmvpmpGqk4sRA09j.jpg)
AI can generate physics-based models for interactive exploration of designs across scales.
We have arrived at the age of self-revising, adaptive intelligence
The most capable systems behave like a malleable network - an or

item.content:encoded:
Rest of World (@restofworld)

Former Hugging Face executive Tiezhen Wang explains how open-source AI training algorithms from Chinese labs are quietly becoming the default infrastructure for U.S. researchers https://restofworld.org/2026/tiezhen-wang-china-us-open-source-ai/?utm_campaign=row-social

🔗 OpenAI or Deepseek? Role of China’s open-source in the AI race - Rest of World

As the U.S. and China battle for artificial intelligence supremacy, a fundamental divide in engineering philosophy could determine the winner.
While American pioneers like OpenAI and Anthropic favor a closed-source approach — keeping their proprietary model code locked behind a commercial interface — Chinese AI labs are aggressively releasing open-source models. This strategy allows developers to download, inspect, and deeply customize the underlying code for free, rather than remaining dependent on an American tech giant’s ecosystem.
Tiezhen Wang, former head of the Asia-Pacific ecosystem at AI community collaboration platform Hugging Face, has observed this trend over the years. Before he moved on from Hugging Face in May, he assisted AI labs in the region in launching open-source models, and helped researchers make their models easier for developers to use.
At a Rest of World virtual event, Wang spoke about the history of open-source models, how Chinese AI labs monetize despite not charging for their models, and the debate over model distillation and intellectual property.
The conversation has been edited for length and clarity. A recording of the live Rest of World event is available [here](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gSsR1ezeenk).
What is the role of open-source models in the China-U.S. AI competition?
A lot of people talk about the AI competition. But in the open-source world, we hold a collaborative mindset.
Many open-source releases from the Chinese labs are helping U.S. labs. For example, the reinforcement learning training algorithm from DeepSeek is becoming the default setting for many U.S. research labs. Many Chinese open-source weights are running on U.S. hardware.
It is like helping each other, not competing like a zero-sum game. We can both be winners if we are growing the pie together.
OpenAI and Anthropic have [accused Chinese AI companies](https://restofworld.org/2026/openai-deepseek-distillation-dispute-us-china/) of distilling their models. How do you view this as an open-source advocate? Is this a challenge for Chinese AI labs?
Distillation is a neutral word in the research world. It’s like I’ve read a book, and I’m telling someone what the book is about. The other person also understands what the book is saying. That’s basically distillation.
It has been done a lot in research labs. I don’t think distillation by itself is anything wrong, and I believe people in the U.S. are distilling each other as well. Recently, we have seen Elon Musk admit that xAI [distilled from OpenAI](https://www.wired.com/story/elon-musk-distill-openai-models-partly-xai/).
It is well known that Anthropic and ChatGPT are [crawling the internet](https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/01/27/anthropic-ai-scan-destroy-books/), getting all kinds of information. So it’s interesting to see that those who did not generate knowledge are trying to stop others from reusing that knowledge.
All AI-generated content should have zero copyright, otherwise people who have compute can abuse and generate all kinds of combinations and copyright everything.
How does monetization differ for open-source and closed-source models?
If you open-source your model, it’s hard to make money directly. But you can still make money.
For example, China’s [Kimi released their model for free](https://www.scmp.com/tech/big-tech/article/3350887/moonshot-ai-releases-flagship-model-open-source-push-continues), but their application programming interface and subscription are still in huge demand because they have the best infrastructure support.
Once a model is released as open-source, people have to spend engineering hours to run it. So, on day zero, the research lab that launched the model has an advantage. That’s one way they can make money.
Another way is, for example, Kimi could release a fine-tuned model as open-source, but keep the base models to themselves, which they can sell.
If we want to think about why a research lab would open-source its models, i

🔗 Is AI replacing jobs? Chinese tech giants layoff workforce - Rest of World

Chinese tech giants are quietly shrinking their workforce — echoing a pattern playing out in Silicon Valley.
In 2025, e-commerce major [Alibaba](https://restofworld.org/tag/alibaba)[Alibaba](https://restofworld.org/tag/alibaba)Alibaba, founded in 1999 by Chinese entrepreneur Jack Ma, is one of the most prominent global e-commerce companies that operates platforms like AliExpress, Taobao, and Tmall.[READ MORE](https://restofworld.org/tag/alibaba) reduced its head count by 34% as it continues to [axe its workforce in](https://www.alibabagroup.com/document-1871720871488389120) its offline business units to focus on artificial intelligence and cloud infrastructure. Search giant [Baidu](https://restofworld.org/tag/baidu)[Baidu](https://restofworld.org/tag/baidu)Baidu is a Chinese technology company that operates the country’s biggest search engine and video-streaming service iQiyi.[READ MORE](https://restofworld.org/tag/baidu) ended 2025 with nearly 7% fewer employees, while electric-vehicle maker BYD cut roughly 10% of its workforce. These numbers were disclosed in the companies’ annual reports, filed at the end of March.
While job cuts at tech companies are often framed as part of an AI-driven transformation, Chinese experts point to broader economic pressures — such as a slowing economy, weak consumer demand, and a prolonged property crisis — for these layoffs. The trend also reflects a correction after years of rapid hiring, experts told Rest of World.
“Many of these companies expanded rapidly during the internet boom, hiring at an exponential pace,” said Sun Zhongwei, a public administration professor at South China Normal University. “The changes in their organization structure are much more about adjusting to a downturn after that cycle of growth than being about AI displacing jobs.”
A former Baidu employee, who was laid off from the marketing department in March, told Rest of World that financial pressure was the reason the company gave her. “Since last year, the company has been cutting people in so-called non-core departments. I saw it coming,” she said, requesting anonymity to protect her future employment opportunities.
Alibaba, Baidu, [Tencent](https://restofworld.org/tag/tencent)[Tencent](https://restofworld.org/tag/tencent)Best known for its super-app WeChat, Tencent is a Chinese technology conglomerate and a major player in the video gaming industry.[READ MORE](https://restofworld.org/tag/tencent), and BYD did not respond to Rest of World’s request for comment for this piece.
“Inevitable” layoffs
Chinese tech companies sit at the center of Beijing’s economic strategy as it competes with the U.S. in advanced technologies. Layoffs by these companies are in line with their U.S. counterparts, which have been cutting jobs while ramping up investment in AI.
Since the start of 2026, tech companies have announced 78,557 job cuts worldwide, of which about 76.7% were by U.S.-based firms, according to an [April report](https://www.rationalfx.com/forex-brokers/tech-industry-layoffs/?) by RationalFX, a U.K.-based financial services firm.  
This month, social media company Snap laid off 16% of its staff — around 1,000 people — and withdrew hundreds of open roles, citing “rapid advancement in AI.” In March, [Oracle shed thousands of employees](https://www.wsj.com/market-data/quotes/AMZN). In 2025, [Amazon cut about 30,000 jobs](https://www.wsj.com/tech/amazon-to-lay-off-around-16-000-corporate-employees-932df0be?mod=article_inline), while [Meta laid off](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-01-13/meta-begins-jobs-cuts-after-shifting-focus-from-metaverse-to-phones) more than 1,000 employees. Meta may reduce its workforce by [another 10% in the near future](https://www.reuters.com/world/meta-targets-may-20-first-wave-layoffs-additional-cuts-later-2026-2026-04-17/). 
The [Chinese government has warned](http://finance.people.com.cn/BIG5/n1/2026/0121/c1004-40649942.html) that AI development would bring “inevitable” job losses d

The first fortunes of the AI era aren't being built by companies. They're being built by single people with one skill and a laptop. No team, no investors, no decade of grinding. That skill is still free to learn, and the market hasn't started charging for it yet.
A new kind of rich person is showing up, and it's confusing everyone.
No team. No investors. No decade of grinding. One person, building alone, worth more in a year than most build in twenty.
They didn't get lucky and they didn't inherit it. They learned one skill before the market knew to charge for it.
That skill turns a single person into the output of a company. The first fortunes built on it are landing now.
Here is the skill, why it pays what it pays, and why the door is still open.
##
The First Fortunes Built By One Person
Something new is happening at the top of the income curve.
Fortunes used to need capital, a team, or a decade. A few people are building them alone, in months.
They aren't coders with a secret. They aren't influencers with a following. They have one skill the market hasn't priced yet.
One person, a laptop, and AI producing the output of a company.
That combination didn't exist three years ago. Now it's minting the first solo fortunes of the era.
##
The One Skill Behind It
Forget prompting. Forget coding. Forget building an audience.
The skill is setting AI up to do real work, then running it the way a company runs staff.
They give AI the full context of what they're building. They point it at the work. They keep it running.
One person directs a stack of AI that produces what used to take a floor of employees.
That's the whole skill, and it's quieter than it sounds.
##
Why It's Possible Now
Three years ago AI could write you a paragraph. It could not run your business.
Now it holds context, plugs into your tools, and works on a schedule you set.
The output that used to require hiring now requires a setup.
A single person can carry a team's output without the payroll that used to cap their income.
The ceiling moved, and almost nobody has noticed.
##
Why It's Still Wide Open
Here is the part that makes it fair. Anyone can learn this skill.
No degree teaches it. No fund backs it. The tools cost about what a subscription costs.
The first people in look like geniuses. They are simply early.
The door is open because the skill is new and the crowd is still prompting.
Early is a choice right now. In two years it won't be.
##
What The Skill Looks Like Today
Strip away the abstraction and the skill has a shape you can build this weekend. It's setting up Claude to run real work.
You give Claude a folder that holds everything about what you're building. You write it a short file that briefs it. You plug in your tools and set a few jobs to run on their own.
The folder is the context. The connectors are the reach. The scheduled tasks are the part that runs without you.
The person who builds that is the one the market is about to pay like a company.
Not a coder. A system builder.
##
Where To Start
The whole thing rests on one skill: setting AI up to produce, not just answer.
[Claude Mastery](https://zephyrhq.gumroad.com/l/ClaudeMastery/Article?utm%5Fsource=Twitter&utm%5Fmedium=Article&utm%5Fcampaign=126)

The self-learning agent that everyone's talking about is not the one your product needs.
The most useful signal of all is actually one that almost nobody captures: the people using your product.
Your agents and users already work side by side, thousands of times a day.
It can learn from each one of these interactions. See the video.
Capturing a live interaction flow between a user and agent for self-learning
This is a guide to all three learning layers & how it’s relevant to you.
Today, agents can learn in three different layers.
For each one: what it is, what it costs, who is actually building it, and whether you even should use self-learning.
You'll see how Anthropic, Karpathy, DeepMind, Microsoft, Hermes, OpenClaw, CopilotKit and others approach self-learning, and where each one stops.
##
Agents can learn in 3 different layers
The cleanest split comes from
[Harrison Chase](https://www.langchain.com/blog/continual-learning-for-ai-agents)
.
* The model = The weights (training parameters)
* The harness = The code around the model (loop, tools, prompts)
* The context = The memory and skills outside the harness which grow
You already use all three in Claude Code.
The model is Claude, the harness is Claude Code itself, and the context is your CLAUDE.md and your skills. Each layer can get better on its own, without touching the other two.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLk2WoaXYAAaaoM?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/ataiiam/article/2069797329809395978/media/2069745266186477568)
Three learning layers for agents
In a real product, self-learning almost always means the harness or the context, not the model. The model belongs to the labs. The other two are yours.
I will use one example across all three: a support agent that issues refunds.
For each layer, I'll ask two questions: can it learn there, and do you own that learning?
##
Layer 1: The Model
This is the layer everyone pictures, and the one almost no one runs. The agent improves the model itself. Labs do it three ways:
1. edit the training code and keep what raises the score
2. write your own training data and fold it into the weights
3. try many code changes and keep the best one
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLk2fFzXEAAQtkc?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/ataiiam/article/2069797329809395978/media/2069745411514896384)
All three are the same loop, and it only runs when a computer can score the result for free.
Model Approach #1 (Karpathy)
Edit the training code, keep what helps
Karpathy's
[AutoResearch](https://github.com/karpathy/autoresearch)
points a coding agent at a small training setup and runs it overnight. It edits one file, trains for five minutes, and scores the result. It keeps the change or undoes it. Then it repeats, a hundred times before you wake up.
One run found a real speedup, about 11 percent.
The catch: The agent improved a different, smaller model. Its own weights never actually changed.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLk3OhLWAAATDkI?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/ataiiam/article/2069797329809395978/media/2069746226317099008)
Model Approach #2 (MIT SEAL)
Write your own training data, apply it as a weight update
[Self-Adapting LLMs (SEAL)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10943)
writes its own training data, trains on it, and keeps what raised the score. These are

item.content:encoded:
Vercel Developers (@vercel_dev)

To ensure coding agents live up to our design standards, we built a system with a skill, linters, evals, and an updating loop.

Learn how we did it and how to build your own ↓
https://vercel.com/blog/teaching-agents-product-design-at-vercel

🔗 Teaching agents product design at Vercel - Vercel

Coding agents can produce working UI fast, but what's harder is a different shape. They can copy your product's style, match its patterns, and try to follow its conventions. What they cannot do is understand why those patterns exist. Code shows agents what shipped, not why one component, phrase, or interaction became your standard. That reasoning lives in design reviews, PR comments, Slack threads, and with the people who were in the room. For an agent, context that isn't in the codebase doesn't exist.
Vercel is an agent-native team. We treat accepted product decisions like code, keeping them in the repository, reviewing changes against them, and making them available to every agent working there.
The way we do this is through product-design. It's a system with three parts:
- An agent skill that gives coding agents the context behind decisions that require product or codebase judgment.
- Linters that enforce clear rules automatically.
- A review loop that gathers evidence from Slack, Figma, and GitHub, then prepares guideline updates for review.
Any team can build the same structure around their own standards.
[Link to heading](https://vercel.com#inside-the-product-design-skill)Inside the product-design skill
The skill lives inside the repository alongside the code it governs. Here's a simplified view of its structure:
repository/├── AGENTS.md├── .agents/│ └── skills/│ └── product-design/│ ├── AGENTS.md│ ├── SKILL.md│ ├── references/│ │ ├── product-judgment.md│ │ ├── interface-quality.md│ │ ├── resilience.md│ │ ├── surfaces.md│ │ ├── surfaces-{surface}.md│ │ ├── copy.md│ │ ├── rules.md│ │ ├── glossary.md│ │ ├── patterns.md│ │ └── coverage-gaps.md│ └── exemplars/│ └── pr-{name}.md└── tooling/ └── scripts/ └── copywriting-eval/ ├── fixtures.json ├── rules-checklist.json └── <fixture>/ ├── before/ └── after/The product-design skill structure inside the repository.
- The repository - AGENTS.mdtells coding agents when to load the skill. The skill-local- AGENTS.mddefines load order, validation, and governance.- SKILL.mdowns the runtime workflow.
- references/stores product-judgment, interface-quality, resilience, copy, canonical product names, interaction patterns, and surface-specific decisions.
- exemplars/documents decisions worth repeating from shipped pull requests, along with mistakes to avoid.- coverage-gaps.mdlists areas where we do not have a standard yet.
- copywriting-eval/tests copy and interface-language behavior. It does not evaluate the broader product-design workflow.
[Link to heading](https://vercel.com#how-the-skill-routes)How the skill routes
SKILL.md resolves the request mode first: shape, implement, review, copy, or harden. This keeps audits from becoming edits and copy passes from expanding into redesigns. It skips backend-only work, telemetry, console errors, generated files, and tests with no shipped UI impact.
The skill routes to canonical sources instead of duplicating them. Component APIs, design-system rules, accessibility criteria, and interaction guidance stay with their owners.
Routing is specific to both task and surface. Material changes load product-judgment and interface-quality first. Copy, component, layout, interaction, accessibility, and resilience work each route to focused references. A modal loads destructive-action patterns and canonical verbs. A settings form loads labels, validation, progressive disclosure, and accessible-name guidance.
You can use this simplified structure as a starting point and replace the paths and standards with your own:
---name: product-designdescription: >- Single entry point for product design and user-facing product implementation in apps/vercel-site. Use whenever work changes what a user sees, understands,
